title: Application foundation, shared-password auth, and relative routing

history.detail:
PASS: QA1 STATIC AUDIT — SPRINT 1 — VERDICT: PASS
Audited commit f2759970d7f1de21bb5d6092f51452475b609606 (working tree clean; committed code, not a working-tree diff).
Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict. No cross-version ("arrives between release A and B") acceptance criterion in this sprint, so that check does not apply.

REQUIREMENTS COVERAGE — 10/10 MET
1. Express/Node 24, single entry point, EJS server-rendered, no bundler — MET. src/server.js -> src/app.js. No frontend build step, no framework creep. Node v24.20.0 confirmed on this machine.
2. Env config + .env.example + .env gitignored — MET. .env.example documents all four vars (PORT, BASE_PATH, SESSION_SECRET, TEAM_PASSWORD_HASH) with generation instructions. .gitignore excludes .env; confirmed .env is NOT tracked by git. Grepped all tracked source for bcrypt-hash literals and secret-shaped assignments: only hit is a synthetic test fixture ('$2a$12$abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv', test/config.test.js:10), not a real hash. No plaintext password anywhere in the repo.
3. BASE_PATH routing via a single url() helper — MET, and verified live, not just read. Ran the app at BASE_PATH=/content-check and read the rendered HTML: href="/content-check/style.css", action="/content-check/login", action="/content-check/logout". Grep for absolute internal paths (href="/, action="/, src="/) outside the helper in views/ returns nothing. All five redirects in src/ go through urlHelper(). Bare /content-check (no trailing slash) 301s to /content-check/ correctly.
4. bcrypt verify, never string equality — MET. src/routes/auth.js:43 uses bcrypt.compare against TEAM_PASSWORD_HASH. No plaintext comparison path exists.
5. httpOnly + SameSite=Lax session cookie; hard startup failure on missing SESSION_SECRET — MET, verified directly. Observed Set-Cookie: content-checker.sid=...; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax. Startup failure asserted on the printed text, not merely on exit status, across three cases (unset / empty string / whitespace-only), all three printing: "[content-checker] Startup failed: Missing required environment variable: SESSION_SECRET. Set it in your .env file (see .env.example) before starting the app." Exit code 1. No default-secret fallback exists in the code.
6. Protected routes redirect unauthenticated requests to login — MET, verified. GET /content-check/ with no session -> 302, Location: /content-check/login. Not a 500, not a blank page.
7. Generic failure message + rate limit — MET, verified. Wrong password -> 401 with rendered text "Incorrect password. Please try again."; response leaks nothing about length, shape, or closeness. Rate limiter allows exactly 10 attempts then returns 429 on the 11th (attempts 9-10 = 401, 11-12 = 429).
8. Logout destroys session and redirects — MET, verified. POST /logout -> 302 to /content-check/login, and reusing the pre-logout cookie afterwards -> 302 to login. Session is genuinely dead server-side. (See ISSUE 1 for a real but non-blocking defect in the same handler.)
9. npm test / npm run lint / npm start all exist and exit clean — MET. 32 tests pass, 0 fail (exit 0). eslint exit 0. Unit tests for the auth middleware and the url helper are present AND meaningful, not smoke tests: requireAuth is covered for pass-through, absent session, present-but-unauthenticated session, and a non-root BASE_PATH redirect target; the integration suite asserts on the actual Set-Cookie header, on the 302 Location, on rendered message text, and includes negative assertions (doesNotMatch on the real password; doesNotMatch on any href/action escaping the BASE_PATH prefix). This is the standard I want to keep seeing.
10. GET /healthz, unauthenticated, under BASE_PATH — MET, verified. /content-check/healthz -> 200 {"status":"ok"} with no session. Mounted before requireAuth deliberately.

CODE QUALITY
Test coverage: Good. Meaningful scenarios, negative assertions, both root and non-root BASE_PATH exercised. Low bcrypt cost factor in tests (4) is a correct deliberate choice, not sloppiness.
Error handling: Good. No swallowed errors found. The app-level error handler logs full detail server-side and returns a generic message to the client (src/app.js:65-70). Session regeneration on login correctly forwards regenerateErr to next() rather than ignoring it (auth.js:55-59); session.destroy does the same. Session fixation is handled via regenerate() on privilege change — that was not a stated requirement and shows someone was actually thinking.
Standards compliance: Follows CLAUDE.md. CommonJS throughout, consistent 'use strict', dependency-injected factories (createApp/createAuthRouter/createRequireAuth/createUrlHelper) rather than module-level singletons, which is what makes the tests clean. normalizeBasePath is defined once in config.js and reused by url.js rather than redefined.
Security: Sound for this sprint's scope. bcrypt verify, no default secret, httpOnly/SameSite=Lax, generic failure text, rate limiting, session regeneration, EJS default escaping on the rendered error. No injection or XSS surface introduced (no user input reaches a query, a shell, or an unescaped template).

ISSUES FOUND — none block shipping; all are follow-up work
1. [MEDIUM] Dead clearCookie with the wrong cookie name — src/routes/auth.js:78. The session cookie is named 'content-checker.sid' (src/app.js:37) but logout calls res.clearCookie('connect.sid') — express-session's default name, which this app never sets. DEMONSTRATED: observed Set-Cookie on logout is "connect.sid=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT" while the cookie actually in use is content-checker.sid. Consequence is bounded: the session IS destroyed server-side, so there is no auth bypass (verified — the stale cookie 302s to login afterwards). But the line is dead code, and the real cookie is left in the browser rather than cleared. This is a copy-pasted default that nobody read before pasting. Fix: clearCookie('content-checker.sid'). Better: hoist the cookie name to a single shared constant so the two sites cannot drift again.
2. [MEDIUM] Rate-limit response returns JSON to an HTML form, with a message that is actively wrong — src/routes/auth.js:24. Once limited, the browser gets a raw JSON body {"error":"Incorrect password. Please try again."} instead of the rendered login page. DEMONSTRATED: submitting the CORRECT password while rate-limited returns 429 with that same "Incorrect password" text. Telling a user their password is wrong when it is actually right, and dumping JSON into their browser, is a defect on both counts. Fix: a handler that renders the login view with a distinct rate-limited message.
3. [LOW-MEDIUM] Session cookie is not scoped to BASE_PATH — src/app.js:41-45. The cookie is issued with Path=/ (observed). Production is a shared tools domain (tools.wordzite.com/content-check), so every sibling tool on that host will receive this app's session cookie on every request. httpOnly keeps sibling page JS from reading it, but sibling servers still see the session ID. This is the same subpath-hygiene principle requirement 3 is built on, applied to the cookie. Fix: set cookie.path to config.basePath || '/'. Not a stated requirement, so not a gate failure — but it should land before the real deploy sprint.
4. [LOW] Rate limit is X-Forwarded-For-spoofable when the app runs without a proxy — src/app.js:24 sets 'trust proxy', 1. DEMONSTRATED: three requests with forged X-Forwarded-For headers each got a fresh bucket (401 rather than 429) while the un-forged IP was already limited. This is CORRECT for the intended production topology (behind exactly one reverse proxy, where the proxy appends the true client IP as the rightmost entry). It is wrong the moment the app is exposed directly, which is exactly what V1-on-localhost is. Nothing in the README or .env.example documents that coupling. Fix: document the single-proxy assumption, and revisit if the deploy topology ever changes.
5. [LOW] The logout test asserts behavior but not the cleared cookie name — test/app.integration.test.js:109-123. It correctly proves the session is dead, which is the thing that matters, and that is why it passes despite ISSUE 1. Adding an assertion on the cleared cookie name is what would have caught it. Dev Team writes that test, not QA1.

ANSWERS TO DEV TEAM'S QUESTIONS
Q: Hard startup failure on TEAM_PASSWORD_HASH as well as SESSION_SECRET — right call or should it fail soft?
A: Right call. Keep it. Without the hash the app boots into a state where login can never succeed for anyone, and that failure surfaces to every user as "Incorrect password" — a misleading runtime symptom, discovered late, pointing at the wrong cause. Failing at boot with the variable named turns a confusing production incident into a one-line fix before the process is up. Requirement 5 names SESSION_SECRET explicitly because that one has a specific extra hazard (a default secret makes session forgery trivial), not because the other config should be treated as optional. Fail fast on both.
Q: CSRF on the login/logout forms.
A: Correctly out of scope here, and not a gate issue. SameSite=Lax blocks the cookie on cross-site POSTs, so the practical risk on these two forms is low. It stops being low in Sprint 2, when project CRUD adds state-changing authenticated routes. Raise it as scoped work there rather than bolting a token on now.

NOTES ON PROCESS
Working tree was clean and the code was committed before this audit — correct, and it means this verdict is a claim about code that actually exists.
bin/hash-password.js is out of requirements but justified: nothing else could produce a valid TEAM_PASSWORD_HASH. It prints only the hash, never the plaintext. Accepted. One caveat worth knowing: the password is passed as an argv, so it lands in the operator's shell history — worth a line in the README telling people to clear it or use a leading space.
Known limitations (in-memory session and rate-limit stores) were disclosed rather than hidden, and are acceptable for a single-instance V1. They need a real store before any multi-instance deploy.
No sign of the Dev1/Dev2 friction affecting this work. Greenfield, single owner, disciplined. This is fine.

HANDOFF NOTE FOR LIVEQA
If you deliberately test the wrong-password path more than 10 times from the same IP within 15 minutes, you will hit the rate limit and get a raw JSON 429 that reads "Incorrect password. Please try again." That is ISSUE 2 above, already known — do not report it as a new blocker, and do not mistake it for the login being broken. Restart the process to reset the in-memory limiter.
